The Gaussian Moments Conjecture
and the Jacobian ConjectureThanks: The first author was partially supported by NSF grant DMS 13020321302032 and the third author partially by the Simons Foundation Grant-278638278638.

Harm Derksen, Arno Van den Essen and Wenhua Zhao Address: H. Derksen, Department of Mathematics, University of Michigan, USA. Email: hderksen@umich.edu Address: A. van den Essen, Department of Mathematics, Radboud University Nijmegen, The Netherlands. Email: A.vandenEssen@math.ru.nl Address: W. Zhao, Department of Mathematics, Illinois State University, Normal, IL 61761. Email: wzhao@ilstu.edu
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We first propose what we call the Gaussian Moments Conjecture. We then show that the Jacobian Conjecture follows from the Gaussian Moments Conjecture. Note that the the Gaussian Moments Conjecture is a special case of ([11, Conjecture 3.23.2]). The latter conjecture was referred as Moment Vanishing Conjecture in ([9, Conjecture A]) and Integral Conjecture in [6, Conjecture 3.13.1] (for the one-dimensional case). We also give a counter-example to show that ([11, Conjecture 3.2]) fails in general for polynomials in more than two variables.

Key words and phrases: 
Gaussian Moments Conjecture, the Jacobian conjecture, the Image conjecture, MZ spaces (Mathieu subspaces)
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
14R15, 60E05, 33C45

1. Introduction

For a random variable XX we denote its expected value by 𝔼⁡(X){\mathbb{E}}(X). Suppose that X=(X1,…,Xn)X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}) is a random vector with a multi-variate normal distribution. We make the following conjecture:

Conjecture 1.1 (Gaussian Moments Conjecture 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(n)\operatorname{\bf GMC}(n)).

Suppose that P⁡(x1,…,xn)∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]P(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is a complex-valued polynomial such that the moments 𝔼⁡(P​(X)m){\mathbb{E}}(P(X)^{m}) are equal to 00 for all m≥1m\geq 1. Then for every polynomial Q⁡(x1,…,xn)∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]Q(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] we have 𝔼⁡(P​(X)m​Q​(X))=0{\mathbb{E}}(P(X)^{m}Q(X))=0 for m≫0m\gg 0.

By using translations and linear maps, we can normalize the random vector XX such that X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n} are independent, with mean 0 and variance 1.

The Gaussian Moments Conjecture is a special case of [11, Conjecture 3.23.2]. Furthermore, because of Proposition 3.33.3 and relation (3.2)(3.2) in [11], the Gaussian Moments Conjecture is the special case of [11, Conjecture 3.13.1] for Hermite polynomials. Note that ([11, Conjecture 3.2]) was later referred as Moment Vanishing Conjecture in ([9, Conjecture A]), and Integral Conjecture in [6, Conjecture 3.13.1] (for one-dimensional case). Unfortunately, this conjecture is false in general, as can be seen from the following

Proposition 1.2.

Let B={(x,y)∈ℝ2|y≥0,x2+y2≤1}B=\{(x,y)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\,|\,y\geq 0,\,x^{2}+y^{2}\leq 1\}, P⁡(x,y)=(x+i​y)2P(x,y)=(x+iy)^{2} and Q⁡(x,y)=x+i​yQ(x,y)=x+iy. Then ∫BP​(x,y)m​𝑑x​𝑑y=0\int_{B}P(x,y)^{m}\,dxdy=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1, but ∫BQ⁡(x,y)​P​(x,y)m​𝑑x​𝑑y≠0\int_{B}Q(x,y)P(x,y)^{m}\,dxdy\neq 0 for all m≥1m\geq 1.

Proof.

For each m≥1m\geq 1, by using the polar coordinates (r,θ)(r,\theta) we have

∫BP​(x,y)m​𝑑x​𝑑y=∫01∫0πr2​m​e2​m​i​θ​r​𝑑r​𝑑θ=0;\int_{B}P(x,y)^{m}\,dxdy=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{\pi}r^{2m}e^{2mi\theta}r\,drd\theta=0;
∫BQ⁡(x,y)​P​(x,y)m​𝑑x​𝑑y\displaystyle\int_{B}Q(x,y)P(x,y)^{m}\,dxdy =∫01∫0πr2​m+1​e(2​m+1)​i​θ​r​𝑑r​𝑑θ\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{\pi}r^{2m+1}e^{(2m+1)i\theta}r\,drd\theta
=2​i(2​m+3)​(2​m+1)≠0.\displaystyle=\frac{2i}{(2m+3)(2m+1)}\neq 0.

∎

Remark 1.3.

Note that Conjecture 3.23.2 in [11] is still open for univariate polynomials. It is also open for the (whole) disks or squares centered at the origin for polynomials in two variables.

Remark 1.4.

The function X12+X22X_{1}^{2}+X_{2}^{2} has an exponential distribution and more generally, X12+⋯+X2​k2X_{1}^{2}+\cdots+X_{2k}^{2} has a χ2\chi^{2} distribution. So, if the Gaussian Moments Conjecture is true for all n≥1n\geq 1, then the conjecture is also true when we replace the Gaussian distributions by exponential or χ2\chi^{2} distributions. The Moments Conjecture for exponential distributions is equivalent to [5, Conjecture 4.1], which is a weaker form of the Factorial Conjecture ([5, Conjecture 4.2]).

One of the main open conjectures in affine algebraic geometry is the notorious Jacobian Conjecture, which was first proposed by O. H. Keller [7] in 19391939. See also [1] and [3].

Conjecture 1.5 (Jacobian Conjecture 𝐉𝐂⁡(n){\bf JC}(n)).

If F:ℂn→ℂnF:{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{C}}^{n} is a polynomial map that is locally invertible, then it is globally invertible.

The main result of this paper is:

Theorem 1.6.

If 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(n){\bf GMC}(n) is true for all n≥1n\geq 1, then 𝐉𝐂⁡(n){\bf JC}(n) is true for all n≥1n\geq 1.

Acknowledgment The main results of the paper were obtained when the authors organized and attended the two-week International Short-School/Conference on Affine Algebraic Geometry and the Jacobian Conjecture, which was supported by and hold at Chern Institute of Mathematics, Tianjin, China from July 14-25, 2014. The authors are very grateful to the institute for supports and hospitality.

2. Background

Suppose that AA is a unital commutative ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-algebra.

Definition 2.1.

A Mathieu-Zhao space (or MZ space) is a ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-linear subspace V⊆AV\subseteq A with the property that fm∈Vf^{m}\in V for all m≥1m\geq 1 implies that for every g∈Ag\in A, fm​g∈Vf^{m}g\in V for m≫0m\gg 0.

Observe that in this definition we have changed the name Mathieu subspace, which was introduced by the third author in [11, 12], into Mathieu-Zhao space or MZ space. This follows a suggestion of the second author in [4]. For some more general studies of this new notion, see [12].

With the definition above we can now reformulate our main conjecture as follows.

Conjecture 2.2 (𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(n){\bf GMC}(n), reformulation).

The subspace

{P⁡(x1,…,xn)∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]∣𝔼⁡(P⁡(X1,…,Xn))=0}\{P(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\mid{\mathbb{E}}(P(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}))=0\}

is an MZ space of  ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Suppose that GG is a complex reductive algebraic group acting regularly on an affine variety ZZ. Then GG also acts on the ring ℂ⁡[Z]{\mathbb{C}}[Z] of polynomial functions on ZZ. Let K⊆GK\subseteq G be a maximal compact subgroup. Then KK is Zariski dense in GG. The Reynolds operator ℛZ:ℂ⁡[Z]→ℂ{\mathcal{R}}_{Z}:{\mathbb{C}}[Z]\to{\mathbb{C}} is the averaging operator:

ℛZ​(f)=∫g∈Kg⋅f​𝑑μ.{\mathcal{R}}_{Z}(f)=\int_{g\in K}g\cdot f\,d\mu.

where d​μd\mu is the Haar measure on KK, normalized such that ∫K𝑑μ=1\int_{K}d\mu=1.

Conjecture 2.3 (Mathieu Conjecture 𝐌𝐂⁡(Z)\operatorname{\bf MC}(Z)).

The kernel Ker⁡(ℛZ)\operatorname{Ker}({\mathcal{R}}_{Z}) of the Reynolds operator is an MZ space of  ℂ⁡[Z]{\mathbb{C}}[Z].

This conjecture is equivalent to the conjecture C⁡(ℂ⁡[Z])C({\mathbb{C}}[Z]) of [8] (see [8, Corollary 1.3]). The group GG acts on its own coordinate ring, and 𝐌𝐂⁡(G)\operatorname{\bf MC}(G) implies 𝐌𝐂⁡(Z)\operatorname{\bf MC}(Z) ([8, Corollary 1.7]). The following theorem was proven in [8, Theorem 5.5]:

Theorem 2.4 (Mathieu).

If 𝐌𝐂⁡(SLn⁡(ℂ)/GLn−1⁡(ℂ))\operatorname{\bf MC}(\operatorname{SL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})/\operatorname{GL}_{n-1}({\mathbb{C}})) is true for all n≥1n\geq 1, then 𝐉𝐂⁡(n){\bf JC}(n) is true for all n≥1n\geq 1.

For later purposes, here we also point out that J. Duistermaat and W. van der Kallen [2] in 19981998 had proved the Mathieu conjecture for the case of tori, which can be re-stated in terms of MZ spaces as follows.

Theorem 2.5 (Duistermaat and van der Kallen).

Let x=(x1,x2,…,xn)x=(x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}) be nn commutative free variables and MM the subspace of the Laurent polynomial algebra ℂ⁡[x1−1,…,xn−1,x1,…,xn]{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1}^{-1},\dots,x_{n}^{-1},x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] consisting of the Laurent polynomials with no constant term. Then MM is an MZ space of ℂ⁡[x1−1,…,xn−1,x1,…,xn]{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1}^{-1},\dots,x_{n}^{-1},x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Let ∂i=∂∂zi\partial_{i}=\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}} be the partial derivative with respect to ziz_{i}. Define

ℰn:ℂ⁡[w,z]=ℂ⁡[w1,…,wn,z1,…,zn]→ℂ⁡[z]{\mathcal{E}}_{n}:{\mathbb{C}}[w,z]={\mathbb{C}}[w_{1},\dots,w_{n},z_{1},\dots,z_{n}]\to{\mathbb{C}}[z]

such that

ℰn​(P⁡(w)​Q​(z))=P⁡(∂)​Q​(z)∈ℂ⁡[z].{\mathcal{E}}_{n}\big(P(w)Q(z)\big)=P(\partial)Q(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z].

Zhao made the following conjecture in [10]:

Conjecture 2.6 (Special Image Conjecture 𝐒𝐈𝐂⁡(n){\bf SIC}(n)).

Ker⁡(ℰn)\operatorname{Ker}({\mathcal{E}}_{n}) is an MZ space of  ℂ⁡[w,z]{\mathbb{C}}[w,z].

Zhao proved the following result ([10, Theorem 3.6, Theorem 3.7]):

Theorem 2.7 (Zhao).

If  𝐒𝐈𝐂⁡(n){\bf SIC}(n) is true for all n≥1n\geq 1, then 𝐉𝐂⁡(n){\bf JC}(n) is true for all n≥1n\geq 1.

3. Reduction of the Jacobian Conjecture to the Gaussian Moments Conjecture

We define the linear map

ℱn:ℂ⁡[w,z]=ℂ⁡[w1,…,wn,z1,…,zn]→ℂ{\mathcal{F}}_{n}:{\mathbb{C}}[w,z]={\mathbb{C}}[w_{1},\dots,w_{n},z_{1},\dots,z_{n}]\to{\mathbb{C}}

by setting

ℱn​(P)=ℰn​(P)∣z=0.{\mathcal{F}}_{n}(P)={\mathcal{E}}_{n}(P)\mid_{z=0}.

For α=(α1,…,αn)∈ℕn\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, set zα=z1α1⋯znαnz^{\alpha}=z_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots z_{n}^{\alpha_{n}} and α!=α1!α2!⋯αn!\alpha!=\alpha_{1}!\alpha_{2}!\cdots\alpha_{n}!. Then we have

ℱn​(wα​zβ)={α!if α=β;0if α≠β.{\mathcal{F}}_{n}(w^{\alpha}z^{\beta})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\alpha!&\mbox{if $\alpha=\beta$;}\\ 0&\mbox{if $\alpha\neq\beta$.}\end{array}\right.
Proposition 3.1.

If Ker⁡(ℱn)\operatorname{Ker}({\mathcal{F}}_{n}) is an MZ space of ℂ⁡[w,z]{\mathbb{C}}[w,z], then Ker⁡(ℰn)\operatorname{Ker}({\mathcal{E}}_{n}) is an MZ space of ℂ⁡[w,z]{\mathbb{C}}[w,z], i.e. 𝐒𝐈𝐂⁡(n){\bf SIC}(n) is true.

Proof.

Assume that Pm∈Ker⁡(ℰn)P^{m}\in\operatorname{Ker}({\mathcal{E}}_{n}) for m≥1m\geq 1. Then for each α∈ℂn\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n} we have

ℰn​(Pm​(w,z))∣z=α=ℰn​(Pm​(w,z+α))∣z=0=ℱn​(Pm​(w,z+α))=0.{\mathcal{E}}_{n}(P^{m}(w,z))\mid_{z=\alpha}={\mathcal{E}}_{n}(P^{m}(w,z+\alpha))\mid_{z=0}={\mathcal{F}}_{n}(P^{m}(w,z+\alpha))=0.

Hence Pm​(w,z+α)∈Ker⁡(ℱn)P^{m}(w,z+\alpha)\in\operatorname{Ker}({\mathcal{F}}_{n}) for all m≥1m\geq 1. Since Ker⁡(ℱn)\operatorname{Ker}({\mathcal{F}}_{n}) is an MZ space of ℂ⁡[w,z]{\mathbb{C}}[w,z], for any Q∈ℂ⁡[w,z]Q\in{\mathbb{C}}[w,z] and α∈ℂn\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n} we have Q⁡(w,z+α)​P​(w,z+α)m∈ker⁡(ℱn)Q(w,z+\alpha)P(w,z+\alpha)^{m}\in\ker({\mathcal{F}}_{n}) for all m≫0m\gg 0. Therefore, for all m≫0m\gg 0 we have

ℰn​(Q⁡(w,z)​P​(w,z)m)∣z=α=ℱn​(Q⁡(w,z+α)​P​(w,z+α)m)=0.{\mathcal{E}}_{n}(Q(w,z)P(w,z)^{m})\mid_{z=\alpha}={\mathcal{F}}_{n}(Q(w,z+\alpha)P(w,z+\alpha)^{m})=0.

Define ZN⊆ℂnZ_{N}\subseteq{\mathbb{C}}^{n} to be the zero set of all ℰn​(Q⁡(w,z)​P​(w,z)m){\mathcal{E}}_{n}(Q(w,z)P(w,z)^{m}) with m≥Nm\geq N. Clearly, ZNZ_{N} is Zariski closed for all NN, and ⋃N=1∞ZN=ℂn\bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty}Z_{N}={\mathbb{C}}^{n}. It follows that ZN=ℂnZ_{N}={\mathbb{C}}^{n} for some integer NN, because a countable union of Zariski closed proper subsets cannot be the whole affine space. So for m≥Nm\geq N, ℰn​(Q⁡(w,z)​P​(w,z)m){\mathcal{E}}_{n}(Q(w,z)P(w,z)^{m}) is the zero function. ∎

Proposition 3.2.

If 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(2​n){\bf GMC}(2n) is true, then Ker⁡(ℱn)\operatorname{Ker}({\mathcal{F}}_{n}) is an MZ space of ℂ⁡[w,z]{\mathbb{C}}[w,z].

Proof.

Let X1,…,Xn,X_{1},\dots,X_{n}, Y1,…,YnY_{1},\dots,Y_{n} are 2​n2n independent random variables with the normal distribution and with mean 00 and variance 11. Define complex-valued random variables WjW_{j}, ZjZ_{j} and real-valued random variables RjR_{j} and TjT_{j} by

Wj=Xj−Yj​i2=Rj​e−i​Tj​ and ​Zj=Xj+Yj​i2=Rj​ei​Tj.W_{j}=\frac{X_{j}-Y_{j}i}{\sqrt{2}}=R_{j}e^{-iT_{j}}\mbox{ and }Z_{j}=\frac{X_{j}+Y_{j}i}{\sqrt{2}}=R_{j}e^{iT_{j}}.

Then R1,…,Rn,T1,…,TnR_{1},\dots,R_{n},T_{1},\dots,T_{n} are independent, and for every 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n, Rj2R_{j}^{2} has an exponential distribution with mean 11 and 𝔼⁡(Rj2​k)=k!{\mathbb{E}}(R_{j}^{2k})=k!. Now consider

𝔼⁡(Wα​Zβ)=𝔼⁡(Rα+β​ei​∑j(βj−αj)​Tj)=∏j=1n(𝔼⁡(Rαj+βj)​𝔼​(ei⁡(βj−αj)​Tj)).{\mathbb{E}}(W^{\alpha}Z^{\beta})={\mathbb{E}}(R^{\alpha+\beta}e^{i\sum_{j}(\beta_{j}-\alpha_{j})T_{j}})=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\Big({\mathbb{E}}(R^{\alpha_{j}+\beta_{j}}){\mathbb{E}}(e^{i(\beta_{j}-\alpha_{j})T_{j}})\Big).

If β≠α\beta\neq\alpha, then βj≠αj\beta_{j}\neq\alpha_{j} for some jj, whence 𝔼⁡(ei⁡(βj−αj)​Tj)=0{\mathbb{E}}(e^{i(\beta_{j}-\alpha_{j})T_{j}})=0 and 𝔼⁡(Wα​Zβ)=0{\mathbb{E}}(W^{\alpha}Z^{\beta})=0. If α=β\alpha=\beta, then we have

𝔼⁡(Wα​Zα)=𝔼⁡(R2​α)=∏j𝔼⁡(Rj2​αj)=∏jαj!=α!{\mathbb{E}}(W^{\alpha}Z^{\alpha})={\mathbb{E}}(R^{2\alpha})=\prod_{j}{\mathbb{E}}(R_{j}^{2\alpha_{j}})=\prod_{j}\alpha_{j}!=\alpha!

It follows that 𝔼⁡(Wα​Zβ)=ℱn​(wα​zβ){\mathbb{E}}(W^{\alpha}Z^{\beta})={\mathcal{F}}_{n}(w^{\alpha}z^{\beta}) for all α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}. By linearity, we get 𝔼⁡(Q⁡(W,Z))=ℱn​(Q⁡(w,z)){\mathbb{E}}(Q(W,Z))={\mathcal{F}}_{n}(Q(w,z)) for every polynomial Q⁡(w,z)∈ℂ⁡[w,z]Q(w,z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[w,z]. It follows readily from 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(2​n){\bf GMC}(2n) that Ker⁡ℱn\operatorname{Ker}{\mathcal{F}}_{n} is an MZ space of ℂ⁡[w,z]{\mathbb{C}}[w,z]. ∎

Now we can prove our main result Theorem 1.6:

Proof of Theorem 1.6.

It follows directly from Proposition 3.1, Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 2.7. ∎

4. Some Special Cases of the Gaussian Moments Conjecture

We view ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] as the coordinate ring of V≅ℂnV\cong{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, where VV is viewed as the standard representation of O⁡(n){\rm O}(n).

Proposition 4.1.

For homogeneous polynomials P⁡(x)P(x), 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(n){\bf GMC}(n) follows from 𝐌𝐂⁡(V){\bf MC}(V).

Proof.

Let Φ:ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]→ℂ\Phi:{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\to{\mathbb{C}} be given by Φ⁡(P⁡(x))=𝔼⁡(P⁡(X))\Phi(P(x))={\mathbb{E}}(P(X)). Any linear map ℂ​[x1,…,xn]d→ℂ{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]_{d}\to{\mathbb{C}} is determined by an element of Sd​(V)S^{d}(V). Since Φ\Phi is invariant under the action of O⁡(n)O(n) it is given by an element of Sd​(V)O⁡(n)S^{d}(V)^{{\rm O}(n)}. But Sd​(V)O⁡(n)S^{d}(V)^{{\rm O}(n)} is at most one dimensional and is spanned by the restriction of the Reynolds operator ℛV{\mathcal{R}}_{V}. So up to a constant, Φ⁡(P​(x)m)\Phi(P(x)^{m}) is equal to ℛV​(P​(x)m){\mathcal{R}}_{V}(P(x)^{m}). If 𝔼⁡(P​(X)m)=0{\mathbb{E}}(P(X)^{m})=0 for m≥1m\geq 1, then ℛV​(P​(X)m)=0{\mathcal{R}}_{V}(P(X)^{m})=0 for m≥1m\geq 1. If Q⁡(x)Q(x) is homogeneous, then ℛV​(P​(x)m​Q​(x))=0{\mathcal{R}}_{V}(P(x)^{m}Q(x))=0 for m≫0m\gg 0. So 𝔼⁡(P​(X)m​Q​(X))=0{\mathbb{E}}(P(X)^{m}Q(X))=0 for m≫0m\gg 0. If Q⁡(X)Q(X) is non-homogeneous then 𝔼⁡(P​(X)m​Q​(X))=0{\mathbb{E}}(P(X)^{m}Q(X))=0 for m≫0m\gg 0, because 𝔼⁡(P⁡(X)​Qd​(X))=0{\mathbb{E}}(P(X)Q_{d}(X))=0 for m≫0m\gg 0 for every homogeneous summand Qd​(x)Q_{d}(x) of Q⁡(x)Q(x). ∎

Proposition 4.2.

Suppose that XX is a Gaussian Random Variable, and P⁡(x)∈ℂ⁡[x]P(x)\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] is a univariate polynomial such that 𝔼⁡(P​(X)m)=0{\mathbb{E}}(P(X)^{m})=0 for m≥1m\geq 1, then P⁡(x)=0P(x)=0. In particular, 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(n){\bf GMC}(n) is true for n=1n=1.

Proof.

As observed in the beginning of this paper, 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(n){\bf GMC}(n) is a special case of the Image Conjecture for Hermite polynomials. For n=1n=1 the case of Hermite polynomials is proved in Corollary 4.3 of [6]. ∎

For a different proof of 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(1){\bf GMC}(1), see Proposition 4.7 and Remark 4.8 of this section.

Proposition 4.3.

Let P∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn]P\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},...,x_{n},\,y_{1},...,y_{n}] such that for each 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n P⁡(x,y)P(x,y) as a polynomial in xkx_{k} and yky_{k} is homogeneous. Then 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(2​n){\bf GMC}(2n) holds for PP.

Proof.

For each 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, let dkd_{k} be the degree of ff as a polynomial in xkx_{k} and yky_{k}.

Making the change of variables for xix_{i} and yiy_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n):

xi=ricosθiandyi=risinθi,x_{i}=r_{i}\cos\theta_{i}\quad\text{and}\quad y_{i}=r_{i}\sin\theta_{i},

we see that P=(r1d1r2d2⋯rndn)FP=(r_{1}^{d_{1}}r_{2}^{d_{2}}\cdots r_{n}^{d_{n}})F for some polynomial FF in cos⁡θi\cos\theta_{i} and sin⁡θi\sin\theta_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n), which is independent on rir_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n).

Let Sn:=(S1)×nS^{n}:=(S^{1})^{\times n}, where S1S^{1} is the unit circle in ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Denote by d​μnd\mu_{n} the measure of dθ1dθ2⋯dθnd\theta_{1}d\theta_{2}\cdots d\theta_{n}, which is a haar measure of the torus SnS_{n}. Then FF can be viewed as SnS^{n}-finite function over the torus SnS^{n}. Furthermore, for any m≥1m\geq 1 we have

(4.1) 𝔼​(Pm​(X,Y))\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}(P^{m}(X,Y)) =∫r1=01⋯∫rn=01(r1m​d1+1⋯rnm​dn+1)(∫SnFmdμn)dr1⋯drn\displaystyle=\int_{r_{1}=0}^{1}\cdots\int_{r_{n}=0}^{1}(r_{1}^{md_{1}+1}\cdots r_{n}^{md_{n}+1})\big(\int_{S^{n}}F^{m}d\mu_{n}\big)\,dr_{1}\cdots dr_{n}
=Am​∫SnFm​d​μn,\displaystyle=A_{m}\int_{S^{n}}F^{m}d\mu_{n},

for some nonzero constant AmA_{m}.

Hence, if 𝔼⁡(Pm)=0{\mathbb{E}}(P^{m})=0 when m≫0m\gg 0, then so is ∫SnFm\int_{S_{n}}F^{m}. Since d​μnd\mu_{n} is a Haar measure of the torus SnS_{n}, applying the Duistermaat-van der Kallen Theorem 2.5 to FF we see that for each polynomial GG in cos⁡θi\cos\theta_{i} and sin⁡θi\sin\theta_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n), we have ∫SnFm​G​d​μn=0\int_{S^{n}}F^{m}G\,d\mu_{n}=0 when m≫0m\gg 0.

Now for each monomial M⁡(x,y)M(x,y) in xix_{i} and yiy_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n), by Eq. (4.1) with PmP^{m} replaced by Pm​MP^{m}M, we see that 𝔼⁡(Pm​M)=0{\mathbb{E}}(P^{m}M)=0 when m≫0m\gg 0. Hence for each polynomial Q⁡(x,y)Q(x,y), we also have 𝔼⁡(Pm​Q)=0{\mathbb{E}}(P^{m}Q)=0 when m≫0m\gg 0. Therefore 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(2​n){\bf GMC}(2n) holds for PP. ∎

Since every homogeneous polynomial in two variables satisfies the condition of Proposition 4.3, we immediately have the following

Corollary 4.4.

𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(2){\bf GMC}(2) holds for all homogeneous polynomials PP.

By a similar argument as in the proof of Proposition 4.3, we have also the following case of Conjecture 3.23.2 in [11]:

Corollary 4.5.

Let BB be the unit disk in ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} centered at the origin with the Lebesgue measure d​x​d​ydxdy. Let P∈ℂ⁡[x,y]P\in{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] such that PP is homogeneous and ∫BPm​𝑑x​𝑑y=0\int_{B}P^{m}\,dxdy=0 for all m≫0m\gg 0. Then for every Q∈ℂ⁡[x,y]Q\in{\mathbb{C}}[x,y] we have ∫BPm​Q​𝑑x​𝑑y=0\int_{B}P^{m}Q\,dxdy=0 for all m≫0m\gg 0.

In the rest of this section we point out that some results proved in [5] for the Factorial Conjecture ([5, Conjecture 4.2]) can also be proved similarly for 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(n){\bf GMC}(n).

First, we give a proof for the following case of 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(n){\bf GMC}(n), which is parallel to [5, Proposition 4.84.8].

Proposition 4.6.

Let F⁡(x)∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]F(x)\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}] such that F⁡(0)≠0F(0)\neq 0. Then 𝔼​(Fm​(X))≠0\mathbb{E}(F^{m}(X))\neq 0 for infinitely many m≥1m\geq 1.

Proof.

Set (−1)!!:=1(-1)!!:=1 and (2k−1)!!:=(2k−1)(2k−3)⋯3⋅1(2k-1)!!:=(2k-1)(2k-3)\cdots 3\cdot 1 for all k≥1k\geq 1. Then for each α∈ℕn\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

Now assume that the proposition fails, i.e., there exists N≥1N\geq 1 such that Φ⁡(Fm)=0\Phi(F^{m})=0 for all m≥Nm\geq N. Since F⁡(0)≠0F(0)\neq 0, replacing FF by F/F⁡(0)F/F(0) we may assume F⁡(0)=1F(0)=1. Note that if ci=0c_{i}=0 for all 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, i.e., F⁡(x)=1F(x)=1, the proposition obviously holds. So we assume ci≠0c_{i}\neq 0 for all 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k. Replacing FF by F2F^{2} we may also assume that 0≠βi∈2​ℕ0\neq\beta_{i}\in 2{\mathbb{N}} for at least one 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k.

Furthermore, by a reduction due to Mitya Boyarchenko (see the proof of [9, Theorem 4.14.1] or [5, Remarks 4.54.5 and 4.64.6]), we may also assume that ci∈ℚ¯c_{i}\in\bar{\mathbb{Q}} for all 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k.

Let B=ℤ⁡[c1,c2,…,ck]B={\mathbb{Z}}[c_{1},c_{2},...,c_{k}] and pp be an odd prime such that p≥Np\geq N and νp​(ci)=0\nu_{p}(c_{i})=0 for all 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, where νp\nu_{p} denotes an extension of the pp-valuation of ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} to BB.

Since each 0≠βi∈2​ℕn0\neq\beta_{i}\in 2{\mathbb{N}}^{n} in the sum above has at least one nonzero (and even) component, so (p​βi−1)!!(p\beta_{i}-1)!! is divisible by pp. Then applying νp\nu_{p} to Eq. (4.3) we get νp​(1)=0\nu_{p}(1)=0, which is a contradiction. ∎

The next proposition is parallel to [5, Proposition 4.104.10].

Proposition 4.7.

Let F⁡(x)=c0​M0+∑i=1dci​MiF(x)=c_{0}M_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{d}c_{i}M_{i} with M0=x1k1⋯xnknM_{0}=x_{1}^{k_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{k_{n}} such that k1≥1k_{1}\geq 1 and k1≥kjk_{1}\geq k_{j} for all 2≤j≤n2\leq j\leq n; ci∈ℂc_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}} (0≤i≤d)(0\leq i\leq d) with c0≠0c_{0}\neq 0; and MiM_{i} (1≤i≤d)(1\leq i\leq d) are monomials in xx that are divisible by x1k1+1x_{1}^{k_{1}+1}. Then 𝔼​(Fm​(X))≠0\mathbb{E}(F^{m}(X))\neq 0 for infinitely many m≥1m\geq 1.

Proof.

Replacing FF by c0−1​Fc_{0}^{-1}F we may assume c0=1c_{0}=1 and replacing FF by F2F^{2} we may assume that k1k_{1} is an even positive integer. Then under these assumptions the proof of [5, Proposition 4.104.10] works through similarly for the linear functional Φ\Phi of ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] given in Eq. (4.2). ∎

Remark 4.8.

Note that when n=1n=1 the conditions of Proposition 4.7 hold automatically for all nonzero univariate polynomials F⁡(x)F(x). Hence 𝐆𝐌𝐂⁡(1){\bf GMC}(1) also follows directly from Proposition 4.7.

Let d≥1d\geq 1 and P⁡(x)=∑i=1nci​xid∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}x_{i}^{d}\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},...,x_{n}] for some ci∈ℂc_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). This proposition can be proved similarly as Proposition 4.164.16 in [5] if we choose the integer mm there to be even, and the prime pp to be (m+2)​d−1(m+2)d-1 or (m+1)​d−1(m+1)d-1, depending dd is odd or even, respectively. Note that the components kik_{i}’s in the proof of Proposition 4.164.16 in [5] for our case must be even when mm is chosen to be even.

5. Moment Vanishing Polynomials

Let again X=(X1,…,Xn)X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}) be a random vector with joint Gaussian distribution. For n≥2n\geq 2, there exist many polynomials P⁡(x)∈ℂ⁡[x]P(x)\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] for which 𝔼⁡(P​(X)m)=0{\mathbb{E}}(P(X)^{m})=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1: if 00 lies in the closure of the O⁡(n)O(n) orbit of P⁡(x)P(x), then 𝔼⁡(P​(x)m)=0{\mathbb{E}}(P(x)^{m})=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1. Indeed, if there exists a sequence of orthogonal matrices A1,A2,…A_{1},A_{2},\dots such that limk→∞P⁡(Ak​(x))=0\lim_{k\to\infty}P(A_{k}(x))=0, then we have 𝔼⁡(P⁡(X))=limk→∞𝔼⁡(P⁡(Ak​(X)))=𝔼⁡(limk→∞P⁡(Ak​(X)))=𝔼⁡(0)=0{\mathbb{E}}(P(X))=\lim_{k\to\infty}{\mathbb{E}}(P(A_{k}(X)))={\mathbb{E}}(\lim_{k\to\infty}P(A_{k}(X)))={\mathbb{E}}(0)=0. A 1-parameter subgroup is a homomorphism λ:ℂ⋆→On​(ℂ)\lambda:{\mathbb{C}}^{\star}\to{\rm O}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) of algebraic groups. We can view λ\lambda as an orthogonal matrix with entries in ℂ⁡[t,t−1]{\mathbb{C}}[t,t^{-1}]. If P​(λ​(t)​(x))P(\lambda(t)(x)) lies in t​ℂ​[t]​[x]t{\mathbb{C}}[t][x], then limt→0P⁡(λ⁡(t)​x)=0\lim_{t\to 0}P(\lambda(t)x)=0 and 00 lies in the closure of the On​(ℂ)O_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) orbit of P⁡(x)P(x). Conversely, the Hilbert-Mumford criterion states that if 00 lies in the On​(ℂ){\rm O}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})-orbit closure of P⁡(x)P(x), then there exists such a 11-parameter subgroup λ:ℂ⋆→On​(ℂ)\lambda:{\mathbb{C}}^{\star}\to{\rm O}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) such that P⁡(λ⁡(t)​(x))∈t​ℂ​[t]​[x]P(\lambda(t)(x))\in t{\mathbb{C}}[t][x]. If Q⁡(x)∈ℂ⁡[x]Q(x)\in{\mathbb{C}}[x], then for large mm, Q⁡(λ⁡(t)​(x))​P​(λ⁡(t)​x)m∈t​ℂ​[t]​[x]Q(\lambda(t)(x))P(\lambda(t)x)^{m}\in t{\mathbb{C}}[t][x] and

𝔼⁡(Q⁡(X)​P​(X)m)=𝔼⁡(limt→0Q⁡(λ⁡(t)​(X))​P​(λ⁡(t)​X)=𝔼⁡(0)=0CLOSE.{\mathbb{E}}(Q(X)P(X)^{m})={\mathbb{E}}(\lim_{t\to 0}Q(\lambda(t)(X))P(\lambda(t)X)={\mathbb{E}}(0)=0.

We make the following conjecture:

Conjecture 5.1.

If 𝔼⁡(P​(X)m)=0{\mathbb{E}}(P(X)^{m})=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1, then there exists a 1-parameter subgroup λ:ℂ⋆→On​(ℂ)\lambda:{\mathbb{C}}^{\star}\to{\rm O}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) such that P⁡(λ⁡(t)​(x))∈t​ℂ​[t]​[x]P(\lambda(t)(x))\in t{\mathbb{C}}[t][x].
